newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND HANDS MOSCOW STRONG PROTEST OVER SHIP.
newsitem.headline: POLAND HANDS MOSCOW STRONG PROTEST OVER SHIP.

text.p: Poland on Thursday handed Russia an official protest note, unprecedented in their recent relations, demanding fast release of a detained Polish fishing trawler and a full explanation, the foreign ministry said.
Spokesman Pawel Dobrowolski told Reuters the government-to-government note had been given to Russia's ambassador to Warsaw in the foreign ministry building.
"It clearly demanded the release of the ship and a full explanation to be provided," Dobrowolski said.
Despite some previous tensions in relations with Moscow, Poland has never before issued Russia this calibre of protest.

The decision followed repeated bids to secure the release of the Aquarius, which was arrested on February 26 by Russian fishery protection and border officials on the Sea of Okhotsk off Russia's Far East.

On Thursday the ship remained under detention in the port of Pietropavlovsk in Kamchatka, where it was brought under armed guard, despite successive assurances from Moscow's foreign ministry that it was about to be freed.

Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, who has appealed without success to his Moscow counterpart Viktor Chernomyrdin to resolve the issue, said on Tuesday that Poland was considering the tough official protest.
But he urged caution, saying that the incident may have been fomented within Russia to harm bilateral ties at a highly sensitive moment in Poland's approach to NATO entry.

Poland seeks good, quiet relations with Russia which will help its bid to join the pact, as Western countries want to avoid NATO enlargement increasing friction with Moscow which portrays the process as a threat to its own security.
Cimoszewicz said he hoped that delay in releasing the ship stemmed simply from chaos in Russia's administration and that authorities on Kamchatka were defying Moscow's orders.
Thursday's note showed hopes of a breakthrough had faded.

Russian officials, who say the ship began fishing a day earlier than its permit allowed and allege irregularities in documentation, want to fine the vessel or even confiscate its catch worth more than $1.2 million, Polish reports say.
They have submitted the case to a local court.
The ship's owners deny wrongdoing, argue that the detention of the ship and other Russian actions infringed a fishery agreeement between the two countries, and want compensation.

Poland's Dobrowolski said the lengthy protest note set out the whole history of the incident, demanded release of the ship, and quoted a July 1995 Polish-Russian agreement on fishing, which laid out methods of resolving such disputes.
